methodology: The review discusses different strategies for the design of star-shaped poly(2-oxazoline) (POx) polymers, focusing on the cationic ring-opening polymerisation (CROP) method as a tool to achieve cross-linked or branched structures. It also explores combinations of CROP with other controlled polymerization techniques.
research_objective: To summarise different strategies for designing star-shaped poly(2-oxazoline) polymers and highlight their potential applications in biomedical fields, particularly in reducing renal clearance and improving blood circulation times.

key_findings.finding: Cationic ring-opening polymerisation (CROP) of 2-oxazolines is presented as a manifold tool to obtain cross-linked or branched star-like materials.
Star-shaped POx are showcased as a versatile platform to create high molar mass POx in a controlled manner and tune the properties of the resulting polymers.
The preparation of star-shaped polymers via the core-first method involves a multifunctional core that acts as the initiator to propagate multiple arms simultaneously.
One obvious advantage of cross-linked POx, such as star-shaped structures, is the ability to produce materials with a defined number of arms and degree of polymerisation in each arm.
The use of multifunctional initiators with different cores can lead to better polymerisation outcomes, such as achieving high monomer conversion and defined polymers.

Polymerisation using porphyrin-cored tetra-tosylate initiators resulted in star-like polymers with broad dispersity (Ð >3), highlighting the importance of initiator design for controlling polymer structure and properties.
The use of multifunctional CROP initiators with controlled polymerization yields star-shaped polymers with reasonable narrow dispersity.

Conclusion and future perspective During the last decade, research on the preparation of star-shaped POx has intensified, leading to the development of highly defined polymer materials with unique properties. Synthetic properties explored include arm-first, core-first, and grafting onto approaches. In particular, the versatility of the CROP enables the preparation of sophisticated materials during the polymerisation, via post-polymerisation modifica- tion, or the combination with other polymerisation techniques. While the synthesis of various systems has been reported in the past, their characterisation and application remains limited. The vast majority of studies, which go beyond synthetic development, investigated the thermo-responsiveness of star-shaped POx. In contrast, the examination of the biological properties often solely concerns their biocompatibility. While only few studies have shown their potential as drug carriers, the unique material properties of star-shaped POx make them ideal candi- dates for further investigations in this area. In the future, star-shaped POx, could serve as drug-delivery vectors with improved site- specificity and reduced site-effects.
